title: Should you vibe code your own AI demo agent?
summary: You can vibe code an AI demo agent in a weekend. Running one in front of buyers means logins, bot walls, sandboxes, guardrails, CRM handoff and upkeep.
body_markdown:
**Can you vibe code your own AI demo agent?** You can build one that works in a weekend. Getting it in front of real buyers, on your real product, every day, is a different project. Your pipeline depends on that second project.


Here's what that second project involves, and how hard each part is:


Consideration What it takes How hard


Driving your live product Logins, authenticator codes, bot protection and flows that survive UI changes Very hard


Latency Listening, thinking, speaking and clicking within about a second Very hard


Speech technology A natural voice, turn-taking, interruptions, accents and noise Hard


Sandboxes Realistic demo data that resets after every session and stays in sync with your product Hard


Prompting and guardrails Staying on message, and never inventing prices, features or security claims Hard


Evals Scoring conversations and catching regressions after every prompt or model change Hard


CRM and pipeline handoff Lead capture, enrichment, HubSpot or Salesforce sync and follow-up Medium


Maintenance Re-checking all of the above with every product release and model change Never finished


We hear this a lot from teams evaluating Karumi: "someone on our team could just vibe code this". The instinct makes sense. Coding agents are very good now. Wire an LLM to a headless browser, add a voice API, point it at your app, and by Sunday night something talks and clicks through your product.


We've also watched how it plays out. Teams that built their own came back to us once they saw how hard and expensive the system is to set up and keep running. This post covers what they ran into after the prototype worked.


The prototype only has to work once. The production agent has to work for every buyer, through every release.


## What does a vibe-coded demo agent get right?


The core loop really is easy now. An LLM can read a page, decide what to click and explain what it sees. A voice API can make it talk. A coding agent will scaffold all of it in a few hours.


That's enough for an internal demo. It's not enough for a buyer, because a prototype only has to work once, for someone who wants it to work.


Weekend prototype Agent in front of buyers


Audience Your team, cheering Skeptical buyers who leave on the first glitch


Product state One logged-in session on a laptop Thousands of sessions, each with its own login, data and timing


Conversation Happy-path questions Pricing, competitors, security, "can it do X?"


When it fails A laugh A lost deal and a bad first impression


Lifespan One demo Every day, through every release


Owner Whoever built it on Saturday Needs one, permanently


The gap between those two columns is the real project. And a demo is one place you can't afford to fail in production: when it breaks, it breaks in front of the buyer you most wanted to impress.


## What do you need to master to run one?


A production demo agent isn't one technology. It's at least four, and each is a specialty of its own:


- **Speech technology.** Speech-to-text, text-to-speech, turn-taking, interruptions, accents and background noise. Getting a voice to sound natural, and to know when the buyer has finished talking, is a field in itself.
- **Sandboxes.** A copy of your product with realistic data that resets after every session, stays in sync with what you ship, and never exposes a real customer.
- **Prompting.** Instructions that keep the agent on message, on your product and inside your guardrails across thousands of conversations it has never seen.
- **Evals.** A way to score conversations and catch regressions, so you know a prompt or model change made things better and not worse.


Then there's **latency** , which cuts across all four. In a spoken conversation, a pause of more than a second or so feels broken, and the agent has to listen, think, speak and click a live product inside that budget. Shaving it down means streaming every stage, choosing models for speed as well as quality, and pre-loading pages before the buyer asks. It's critical, and it's one of the hardest parts to get right.


## Why is driving a live product the hard part?


Most of our own engineering time goes here, not into the chat. Showing your real product, rather than a recording, means solving all of this:


- **Logins that fight back.** SSO, email-first screens, magic links, authenticator codes and sessions that expire halfway through a demo. The failure often looks like success: the agent thinks it's in while it's sitting on a login page.
- **Bot protection.** Cloudflare, Akamai and similar tools exist to block automated browsers. Run a script against your own app too often and you can get your demo account locked.
- **Safe demo data.** Buyers shouldn't see real customer records or break a shared account. You need a sandbox that looks real, resets cleanly and never touches production.
- **A UI that keeps changing.** Every release moves buttons and renames pages. Hard-coded clicks break silently, so you need checks that catch a broken flow before a buyer does.
- **Speed.** A demo that waits eight seconds for every page feels broken. Pre-loading, caching and timing the narration over page loads are each their own piece of work.
- **Interruptions.** Real buyers cut in with "wait, go back". The agent has to stop, answer and pick up where it left off.


None of this shows up in a prototype video. All of it shows up in front of a buyer.


## What does it take to make the conversation trustworthy?


A demo agent speaks for your brand. One that makes things up about your product, in front of a buyer, does more harm than no agent at all. Keeping it trustworthy is ongoing work:


- **Grounded answers.** It should answer from your docs, case studies and positioning, and hand off to your team instead of guessing at pricing or the roadmap.
- **Guardrails.** Questions about competitors, discounts, legal or security claims, and attempts to jailbreak it all need deliberate handling.
- **Natural voice.** Low latency, interruptions, silences, and narration that stays in sync with what's on screen.
- **Languages.** If you sell in more than one market, every script, flow and answer has to work in each language.
- **Review.** Someone has to read conversations, score them and fix weak answers every week. Otherwise quality drifts and nobody notices.
- **Security questions.** Your security team will ask where transcripts go and which model providers see them. You need answers before they ask.


## Isn't the agent the whole product?


No. The value of a demo agent is what it does for your pipeline, and homegrown bots usually stop at the conversation. Sales and marketing need everything around it:


- **Entry points per campaign** , so LinkedIn, events, your website and outbound each get their own link, greeting and starting flow, and you can see which channel works.
- **Lead capture and enrichment** : who the visitor is, which company, and whether they fit your ICP.
- **Handoff to your stack** : qualified sessions land in HubSpot or Salesforce with a summary, the right rep gets pinged, and the follow-up goes out on its own.
- **Insight** : the questions buyers ask most, where they drop off, and which objections come up.
- **No-code editing** , so marketing and sales engineers change scripts and flows without filing a ticket.


Each of these is a small product of its own. Build them in-house and your demo bot turns into an internal platform with its own roadmap.


## What does building your own really cost?


Vibe coding makes the first version nearly free. It doesn't make the next hundred versions free, and that's where the cost is.


- **Every product update is a demo update.** Each release can move a button, rename a page or change a flow. Someone has to re-check the journeys, refresh the sandbox, update the scripts and re-run the evals, every time you ship.
- **Someone has to own it.** When the person who built it moves back to the core product, or leaves, the bot quietly breaks. Generated code nobody fully understands is hard to hand over.
- **The stack underneath keeps moving.** LLM, voice and browser-automation vendors change models, prices and APIs every few months. Each change means another round of testing, and often a rewrite.
- **It competes with your roadmap.** Every engineering week spent on the demo bot is a week not spent on the product you actually sell.
- **Time to value.** A working internal build is usually months away from being safe to show buyers. The pipeline that justified the project waits in the meantime.


So the honest comparison isn't a subscription against a weekend of coding. It's a subscription against a part-time engineering team, indefinitely, plus the deals you lose while it's being built.


## When does building it yourself make sense?


Building is the right call when all three of these are true:


1. An AI demo agent is core to what you sell, not a channel for selling something else.
2. You can put a dedicated team on it permanently, not for one sprint.
3. You're fine waiting months before buyers see it.


If not, the most useful thing your team can vibe code is a prototype of what they want. Hand that wish list to a platform that already handles logins, sandboxes, guardrails, voice, analytics and CRM handoff, and spend your engineering time on your own product.


That's what[Karumi](https://karumi.ai/products/videocall-agent) does. The agent learns your product by exploring it, drives it live while it talks to the buyer, and sends every session to your CRM. Most teams are live in two weeks, and we carry the maintenance.


## FAQ


### Can't we start with a prototype and switch later?


You can, and a prototype is a good way to work out what you want. Just budget for the switch: the work after the prototype is where most of the cost is, and buyers who see a broken demo don't come back for a second look.


### What if our product changes every week?


That's the strongest argument against hard-coded flows. Karumi re-learns your product as it changes, so a renamed page or a moved button doesn't take the demo down.


### Do we lose control if we don't build it?


No. Your team writes the scripts, picks the flows and sets the guardrails. What you hand over is the infrastructure: browsers, logins, voice, sandboxes and the integrations.


### How do we compare the two fairly?


Pick one core flow your buyers care about and run both on it for a week: your prototype and a Karumi agent, on the same questions. Count how often each one gets through the demo without a glitch.
